To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) hydrodynamics of a first-order phase transitions is not a trivial extension of hydrodynamics of the second order phase transitions, (2) the hydrodynamics of first order phase transitions is a very complex and interesting subject, (3) the critical point of a first-order transition is not a critical point in the usual sense, and (4) hydrodynamical description is a very powerful tool to study the dynamics of phase transitions.
the critical point is a point of enhanced fluctuations in the thermodynamical approach, but it is a point of suppressed fluctuations in the hydrodynamical approach.

the hydrodynamical description is able to reproduce the thermodynamic behavior of the system in the critical point region and the critical endpoint is not a necessary condition for the enhancement of fluctuations.

the study of the hadron-quart phase transition in heavy ion collisions.
the study of the hydrodynamical evolution of heavy ion collision.
a study of the hydrodynamic properties of a first-order phase transitions, which can be important for understanding of the properties of strongly interacting matter.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the critical endpoint is not a necessary ingredient for the description of the observed fluctuations in the RHIC data.
in the vicinity of the phase boundary the hydrodynamical description is not applicable and a non-equilibrium approach should be used.
the hydrodynamical description with the equation of state with a first order phase transition does not allow for a critical endpoint.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the hydrodynamical approach is a useful tool to study non-equilibrium processes, but in the near-critcal region the thermodynamical approach can be used to obtain qualitative results.

the hydrodynamical approach does not predict a significant enhancement of fluctuations in heavy-ion collisions at RHIC and LHC energies, which is in contrast to the predictions of thermodynamical approach.
we can not expect a clear signal for a first-order transition in heavy-ion experiments.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the critical point in the phase diagram of nuclear matter is unlikely to be seen in the near future in experiments with heavy-ion collisions.
in order to observe critical fluctuations in heavy-ion collisions one needs to study a system with a small viscosity and a small surface tension, which is a very challenging task.
the thermodynamically predicted critical endpoint is an unphysical artifact.
